topics.title: 01 · Why finance exists
topics.subtitle: Risk sharing, incentives & innovation
topics.lesson:
A workshop needs equipment. A saver has money that is not needed immediately. Finance creates agreements that connect them: a loan promises repayments, while shares give the saver ownership. Insurance can separately protect a specified loss.

Start by asking who pays whom, when they pay, and what happens if things go wrong. The point is to make useful activity possible and risks bearable. Hidden information and conflicting incentives explain why understandable contracts and oversight matter.

topics.title: 02 · Risk & portfolios
topics.subtitle: Probability, correlation, CAPM & tails
topics.lesson:
An average gain does not tell you how painful a loss might be. Begin with the possible outcomes, how likely they are, the period they cover and whether the person can afford the downside. A return can be stated in dollars or as a percentage of the starting investment.

Next, look at investments together. Owning more names helps only to the extent that their problems differ. Volatility describes variation around an average; correlation describes joint movement. Neither is a promise that losses cannot occur.

topics.title: 03 · Prices & psychology
topics.subtitle: Efficiency, forecasts, bubbles & narratives
topics.lesson:
A share price reflects what people expect, not just what has already happened. A profitable company can disappoint investors if they expected even more. Stories and the behavior of other investors can influence those expectations.

People also bring reference points and habits to decisions. Holding a loser to reach the purchase price again does not itself improve its prospects. These lessons connect market information with the way people interpret and act on it.

topics.title: 04 · Money, bonds & yields
topics.subtitle: Cash flows first; prices and rates second
topics.lesson:
A bond is a loan represented by a tradable contract. Face value is the principal promised at the end. A coupon is an interest payment in dollars. The coupon rate is an annual percentage of face value used to calculate those payments.

The price paid today can differ from face value. Yield relates the purchase price to promised payments and is usually quoted as a percentage per year under a stated convention. Follow the dollar payments and their dates before applying the formula. Then consider default, changing market rates and inflation.

topics.title: 05 · Stocks & corporations
topics.subtitle: Valuation, ownership & capital structure
topics.lesson:
Buying an ordinary share makes you an owner of a business. You receive a claim on what remains after obligations with higher priority. Its value can rise or fall; it does not promise the return of your purchase price.

Valuation asks what future money could reach investors and what that money is worth today. Earnings ratios help compare price with business results, but they are not promised annual returns. New shares, dividends and buybacks also move money and ownership in different ways.

topics.title: 06 · Housing & mortgages
topics.subtitle: Amortization, prepayment & securitization
topics.lesson:
A home is somewhere to live as well as an asset with an uncertain future sale price. A mortgage adds borrowing, interest payments and a repayment schedule. Compare the money that must leave the household with the value and flexibility it receives.

An investment property produces operating income after ordinary expenses. Cap rate compares that annual income with property value before borrowing costs. Mortgage-backed investments combine home-loan payments, but pooling cannot remove every default or timing risk.

topics.title: 07 · Derivatives & hedging
topics.subtitle: Replication, payoff diagrams & no-arbitrage
topics.lesson:
A derivative is a contract whose payments depend on another price or event. A forward obligates an exchange later at an agreed price. An option gives its buyer a choice, and buying that choice costs a premium.

Separate the payoff at the end from profit after purchase costs. Keep dollars per share distinct from whole-contract dollars. Pricing models compare matching future payments, while practical hedging also needs cash, trading access and attention to assumptions.

topics.title: 08 · Banks & central banks
topics.subtitle: Balance sheets, money creation & resilience
topics.lesson:
A bank owes deposits to customers and holds assets such as loans and securities. Equity is assets minus liabilities: the owners’ remaining stake. Losses reduce that cushion when obligations stay fixed.

Liquidity means finding cash for payments now. Solvency means assets are worth enough to cover obligations. These are different questions. Lending, central-bank operations, capital rules and deposit insurance all interact with them, but no single mechanism removes every risk.

topics.title: 09 · Institutions & trading
topics.subtitle: Funds, intermediaries & market plumbing
topics.lesson:
Different financial firms perform different jobs. A broker acts for a client, a dealer trades for itself, and an investment bank can help a company issue securities. Ask which role the firm is performing and how it is paid.

Funds pool investments, but their trading and withdrawal rules differ. A fund price is dollars per share; annual fees are percentages per year when quoted as expense ratios. The assets inside and the investor’s need for cash matter as much as the product label.

topics.title: 10 · Leverage & crises
topics.subtitle: Funding runs, contagion & resolution
topics.lesson:
Borrowing magnifies the gain or loss on the owner’s own money. A lender may require cash or extra collateral before an investment has time to recover. Forced selling can then lower prices for other holders.

Financial crises often combine losses, fragile funding and common reactions. Look at the path as well as the final value: who needs cash, who can withdraw, who owns similar assets and which services must keep working?

topics.title: 11 · Finance & society
topics.subtitle: Public debt, pensions, ethics & access
topics.lesson:
Finance also organizes public borrowing, retirement income and protection against unemployment or living a long life. The useful question is which risk is shared and who finances the promise.

Government debt compared with GDP is a ratio, while annual interest and growth are rates. Pension promises are payments under particular rules, not all the same kind of investment account. Institutions should be judged by how their arrangements serve people’s needs.

topics.title: 12 · Finance today
topics.subtitle: 2026 context, digital assets, AI & private credit
topics.lesson:
New market structures and technologies still raise familiar questions: what is promised, who must pay, what supports the claim and how quickly can money be returned? A new name or ledger does not remove those questions.

Read regulations with their scope and effective dates. Check whether reported private-asset prices are updated frequently. Treat token rights and model predictions as arrangements to understand, rather than guarantees. The dated source snapshot is identified separately from the teaching examples.

cards.title: Contingent claims
prompts: What makes a financial claim contingent?
Explain contingent claims in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about contingent claims. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A contingent claim pays according to what happens in a future situation.
cards.explanation: Think of a fire policy: it pays if a covered fire occurs. A share depends on the business’s results. To understand the contract, ask who pays whom, after which event, and how much money changes hands.

cards.title: Risk sharing
prompts: How can giving up expected income make a farmer better off?
Explain risk sharing in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about risk sharing. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A farmer may prefer a more dependable income even when the average dollar amount is lower.
cards.explanation: Losing money needed to keep the farm running can be more damaging than an equal extra gain is helpful. Insurance transfers a specified risk for a premium, the price of coverage. Pooling helps when different farmers do not all lose together.

cards.title: Limited liability
prompts: What does limited liability usually mean for a common shareholder?
Explain limited liability in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about limited liability. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: An ordinary shareholder generally risks the money invested, without having to pay company debts from unrelated personal assets.
cards.explanation: The shares can still become worthless. Limited liability limits responsibility for additional company losses; it does not guarantee repayment of the investment. Personal guarantees and legal exceptions must be considered separately.

The government guarantees the shareholder’s investment.

cards.title: Adverse selection
prompts: Why might a voluntarily insured pool contain unusually risky people?
Explain adverse selection in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about adverse selection. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: People who privately know they are more likely to claim may be more eager to buy insurance.
cards.explanation: The insurer may therefore attract a riskier group than it expects. This information problem happens before the agreement. Checking risk and encouraging broad participation can help, but those choices also affect cost and access.
choices: People who privately know they are more likely to claim may be more eager to buy insurance.
Insurance necessarily makes people careless afterward.
Insurers always know every customer’s risk.

cards.title: Moral hazard
prompts: A fully insured owner stops maintaining safety equipment. What problem is this?
Explain moral hazard in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about moral hazard. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: The owner takes less care after obtaining protection. That changed incentive is called moral hazard.
cards.explanation: The insurer pays part of a covered loss, so prevention may feel less worthwhile to the owner. A deductible makes the customer pay part of the loss and can preserve a reason to be careful. Deliberate wrongdoing is not necessary.
choices: The owner takes less care after obtaining protection. That changed incentive is called moral hazard.
Adverse selection before the policy.
A reduction in aggregate risk.
checklist: The owner takes less care after obtaining protection. That changed incentive is called moral hazard.

cards.title: Principal–agent problems
prompts: Why can a bonus tied to this year’s profits hurt a bank’s owners?
Explain principal–agent problems in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about principal–agent problems. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A manager may choose risks that improve this year’s bonus while leaving later losses to the owners.
cards.explanation: One person makes decisions for another but is rewarded on a different timetable. That is a principal–agent problem. Monitoring and pay arrangements can improve alignment, although no contract removes every conflict.
choices: A manager may choose risks that improve this year’s bonus while leaving later losses to the owners.
Managers always bear all future losses.
High profits prove there are no hidden risks.
checklist: A manager may choose risks that improve this year’s bonus while leaving later losses to the owners.

cards.title: Financial innovation
prompts: What test should a useful financial innovation pass?
Explain financial innovation in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about financial innovation. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A useful financial innovation helps people fund worthwhile activity or manage risk after its costs and weaknesses are considered.
cards.explanation: More complicated contracts are not automatically better. Ask what problem the new arrangement solves, who takes the risk, what it costs, and what happens when conditions become difficult.
choices: A useful financial innovation helps people fund worthwhile activity or manage risk after its costs and weaknesses are considered.
It must make every participant richer.
It is useful whenever trading volume rises.

cards.title: Financial externalities
prompts: How can a rational forced asset sale harm other institutions?
Explain financial externalities in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about financial externalities. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A forced sale can lower prices for other holders and lead to further losses and selling.
cards.explanation: The seller may only be trying to raise cash. Other institutions then face lower prices on the same assets. This wider effect is an externality because the original seller does not bear all the costs imposed on others.

The sale automatically destroys all contracts.
Only irrational decisions can create crises.

cards.title: Expected return
prompts: Is an investment’s expected return a guaranteed outcome?
Explain expected return in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about expected return. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Expected return is an average of possible percentage returns, weighted by their probabilities. It is not guaranteed.
cards.explanation: State the period first, such as one year. Multiply each possible return by its chance and add the results. A positive average can coexist with a substantial chance of losing money in the actual year.
choices: Expected return is an average of possible percentage returns, weighted by their probabilities. It is not guaranteed.

cards.title: Variance and volatility
prompts: What does return standard deviation measure?
Explain variance and volatility in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about variance and volatility. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Variance and volatility describe how widely returns vary around their average.
cards.explanation: Variance averages squared differences, so its units are squared return units. Its square root is standard deviation, also called volatility, measured in return units for a stated period. It counts unusually good outcomes as deviations too, and does not describe every extreme loss.
choices: Variance and volatility describe how widely returns vary around their average.
Only permanent losses.
The average return itself.

cards.title: Correlation
prompts: Why can two volatile assets form a less volatile portfolio?
Explain correlation in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about correlation. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Holdings can offset some of each other’s fluctuations when their returns do not move perfectly together.
cards.explanation: Correlation is a unitless number from −1 to +1, not a return percentage. Portfolio risk also depends on the amount invested in each holding and each holding’s volatility. Correlations can change, especially during stress. Zero correlation alone does not establish full statistical independence.
choices: Holdings can offset some of each other’s fluctuations when their returns do not move perfectly together.
Owning two assets guarantees no losses.
Their individual volatilities must fall.

cards.title: Systematic risk
prompts: Can owning many technology shares eliminate recession risk?
Explain systematic risk in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about systematic risk. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Owning many shares can still leave exposure to common industry or economic problems.
cards.explanation: A failed product may mainly hurt one company. A recession can hurt many companies together. Diversification reduces dependence on individual companies, but it does not make the portfolio independent of the economy.
choices: Owning many shares can still leave exposure to common industry or economic problems.
Yes, once you own 100 shares.
Yes, provided every company is profitable.

cards.title: Beta
prompts: Does beta measure all of a stock’s risk?
Explain beta in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about beta. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Beta measures how returns move with a selected market benchmark; it does not measure every risk.
cards.explanation: Beta is unitless. Its estimate depends on the benchmark and measurement period. A low-beta business can still fail for company-specific reasons, or suffer an unusual large loss that a simple market relationship misses.
choices: Beta measures how returns move with a selected market benchmark; it does not measure every risk.
Yes, beta equals total volatility.
No, beta measures only the dividend yield.

cards.title: CAPM
prompts: Which risk does the basic CAPM reward with higher expected returns?
Explain capm in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about capm. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Basic CAPM links required return to shared market exposure, measured by beta.
cards.explanation: CAPM means Capital Asset Pricing Model. It adds beta times the expected market risk premium to a risk-free rate. The rates must refer to the same period, usually percent per year. Real returns can depend on risks and patterns that this simple model omits.
choices: Basic CAPM links required return to shared market exposure, measured by beta.
All company-specific risk equally.
Only the chance of a positive return.

E[ ] means expected value.; Units: Rates are percentages for the same period, commonly per year. Beta is unitless. In a decimal calculation, divide percentages by 100 first.

cards.title: Efficient frontier
prompts: What makes a portfolio efficient in mean–variance theory?
Explain efficient frontier in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about efficient frontier. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: On the modeled efficient frontier, a better expected return requires more volatility, given the available choices.
cards.explanation: Both measures must use a stated time period. The frontier is calculated from estimates and investment restrictions. If those estimates change, the supposedly best portfolio can change too. The model does not promise which holding will perform best in real life.
choices: On the modeled efficient frontier, a better expected return requires more volatility, given the available choices.
It always earns the most in every outcome.
It contains only safe assets.

cards.title: Capital market line
prompts: How does the capital market line differ from the security market line?
Explain capital market line in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about capital market line. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: The capital market line uses total volatility. The security market line uses beta.
cards.explanation: The capital market line concerns efficient portfolios mixing a risk-free asset with a particular risky portfolio. The security market line is CAPM’s expected-return comparison across beta. Beta is unitless; volatility and expected return use stated return periods.

Both use total volatility for every individual stock.
The CML prices only options.

cards.title: Law of large numbers
prompts: When is insurance pooling most effective?
Explain law of large numbers in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about law of large numbers. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Pooling many sufficiently independent losses can make the average loss easier to predict.
cards.explanation: This is the law of large numbers. If one event damages many insured properties together, the losses do not average away. Reinsurance transfers some insurer risk to another insurer; reserves provide resources for claims. Neither prevents the original damage.

When every claim happens at once.
When risks are perfectly positively correlated.

cards.answer: A loss threatening basic needs can hurt more than an equal extra gain would help.

cards.answer: Good results can disappoint if investors expected even better results or a better outlook.

cards.title: Stablecoins

Explain stablecoins in your own words, and give an example.

cards.title: Tokenization

Explain tokenization in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about tokenization. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: Recording a bond as a token does not remove the borrower’s obligation to pay or the possibility of default.
cards.explanation: Tokenization changes how a claim may be recorded or transferred. The holder still needs valid legal rights, reliable custody and a workable settlement process. A ledger entry alone does not automatically establish ownership of an asset that can be redeemed.

cards.title: Backtesting and AI
prompts: Why can an impressive financial backtest fail in live use?
Explain backtesting and ai in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about backtesting and ai. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A good historical backtest can fail in live use because it used hindsight, fitted accidental patterns, ignored costs or relied on relationships that changed.
cards.explanation: Overfitting means learning sample-specific noise. Data leakage uses information unavailable at the real decision time. Test on genuinely unfamiliar data, include realistic execution and examine adaptation by other participants. A historical return percentage is not a promised future annual rate.

cards.title: Cyber and infrastructure concentration
prompts: Why can reliance on a shared critical service create systemic risk?
Explain cyber and infrastructure concentration in your own words, and give an example.
A friend asks about cyber and infrastructure concentration. Explain the main idea and one limitation without using your notes.
cards.answer: A shared operational failure can disrupt several otherwise separate financial firms together.
cards.explanation: Banks and funds can depend on the same payment system, custodian, cloud service or data provider. Independent portfolios can therefore share one operational weakness.
